problem.title: Most agent projects do not fail
problem.body: Projects stall when setup gets unclear: too many stack choices, too many keys, and no simple recovery path when something breaks.

0.label: "I know what I want the agent to do. I still need the fastest sane path to get one working."
0.body: Starting from zero is not the real problem. The real problem is choosing the stack, sequence, and standards without turning the work into endless research.

1.label: "I already built part of this. Now I need to recover the setup instead of restarting from scratch."
1.body: When setup breaks halfway through, you need the next repair step, not another research session.

2.label: "Something is already live, but I do not trust the cost, logic, or failure modes yet."
2.body: At that point it is not enough for the agent to exist. It has to be legible, controllable, and safe enough to touch real work.

3.label: "I need a system I can explain, review, and control before I rely on it."
3.body: If you cannot see runs, thresholds, approvals, and behavior under pressure, you do not have an operational asset yet.

problem.close: Pico turns that uncertainty into one practical next step.

0.q: Do I need to know how to code?
0.a: No. Pico is built to make the next step clear without requiring an agent-engineering background.

1.q: What if I already tried and failed?
1.a: That is the point. Connect the stuck setup and start from the blocker.

2.q: What kind of agent work is this for?
2.a: Support flows, copilots, lead capture, follow-up, and other practical agent workflows.

3.a: Yes. Open onboarding now, continue into Academy, and sign in when you want hosted progress, tutor, or checkout continuity.

4.a: PicoMUTX is the setup-focused entry point into MUTX. Heavier multi-team governance belongs in the broader MUTX stack.

compass.body: Use Tutor only to recover one grounded next move. Return to the lesson when the answer is enough, inspect Autopilot when runtime is the real blocker, and escalate only when neither route can tell the truth.
compass.aside: A good Tutor answer ends in one move. If it does not, leave the loop and return to the lesson, runtime, or support.

items.returnCaption: Return here when the Tutor answer still keeps the lesson route honest.
items.inspectCaption: Open this when the problem has moved from knowable lesson logic to runtime state.
items.escalateCaption: Escalate only when the Tutor answer still does not provide a concrete move.

exitRoute.label: Exit route

compass.title: Use the shortest route that keeps the product honest
compass.body: Keep the first win narrow. Follow the lesson when sequence is clear, use Tutor for one blocked command, open Autopilot only when live runtime state is the real question, and escalate last.
compass.aside: This chapter exists to compress the world, not widen it. First proof should happen before preferences, architecture debates, or tool tours.
compass.primaryCaption: Stay on the current mission until its proof is real.
compass.tutorCaption: Use Tutor when one knowable command or setup step is blocked.
compass.runtimeCaption: Use Autopilot when live runtime state becomes the source of truth.
compass.supportCaption: Escalate only when the product route can no longer resolve the edge honestly.

compass.title: Support exists only to return the operator to the product
compass.body: Escalate cleanly, attach the packet, and return to the surface that can move the work again. Academy handles sequence, Tutor handles a knowable next step, and Autopilot handles live runtime truth.
compass.aside: Human help should resolve the messy edge, not replace the product. The best support interaction ends with a clearer route back into Pico.

standards.label: Escalation standards
standards.title: Hand off the problem like a precise operator

cards.label: 01 • Route
cards.title: Name the stack and surface
cards.body: Say whether the issue belongs to Hermes, OpenClaw, NanoClaw, PicoClaw, Tutor, Academy, Autopilot, or the hosted account lane.

cards.label: 02 • Evidence
cards.title: Attach the proof packet
cards.body: Bring the command, panel state, launcher status, or approval signal that shows exactly where the route stopped.

cards.label: 03 • Return
cards.title: Ask for the route back to motion
cards.body: A good escalation ends with the shortest route back to a lesson, a Tutor answer, or a live control action.

packetPosture.label: Packet posture
packetPosture.body: Strong support starts with a clean packet. The best escalation reads like an operator handoff, not a panic dump.

deskTone.label: Desk tone
deskTone.body: Support should lower the temperature without slowing the route back to action.

bestFirstMove.label: Best first move
bestFirstMove.body: Copy the packet, choose the right lane, and ask for the shortest route back to Academy, Tutor, or Autopilot.

desk.label: Support desk
desk.title: Send context, not noise
desk.body: Human help is for the part the product cannot honestly close by itself. The faster you frame the blocker, the faster support can return you to the product route.

callout.title: If the next move is still obvious, go back and do it.
callout.body: Support exists for the messy edge, not to skip the lesson, Tutor, or the live control surface.

lanes.title: Stack or runtime blocker

cards.title: 3. Return to the product
cards.body: The reply should restore momentum, not create a support maze.
